content: 1. Infants who cannot be fed their mother’s milk or donor human milk and fail to gain weight despite adequate feeding with standard infant formula should be given preterm infant formula. This recommendation is weak and based on low-quality evidence, particularly relevant in resource-limited settings. 2. Low birth weight (LBW) infants, including very low birth weight (VLBW) infants, who cannot be fed their mother’s milk or donor human milk should be fed standard infant formula from the time of discharge until six months of age. This is a weak recommendation supported by low-quality evidence, particularly in resource-limited settings. 3. VLBW infants who are fed their mother’s milk or donor human milk do not require bovine milk-based human milk fortifiers. However, if they fail to gain weight despite adequate breast milk feeding, they should be given human milk fortifiers, preferably those that are human milk-based. This is a weak recommendation based on low to very low-quality evidence. 4. VLBW infants fed their mother’s milk or donor human milk should receive daily calcium supplementation (120–140 mg/kg per day) and phosphorus supplementation (60–90 mg/kg per day) during the first months of life. This is a weak recommendation supported by low-quality evidence. 5. VLBW infants fed their mother’s milk or donor human milk should receive iron supplementation of 2–4 mg/kg per day starting at two weeks of age and continuing until six months of age. This is a weak recommendation based on low-quality evidence. 6. Daily oral vitamin A supplementation is not recommended for LBW infants fed their mother’s milk or donor human milk due to insufficient evidence of benefits. This is a weak recommendation supported by low-quality evidence. 7. Routine zinc supplementation is not recommended for LBW infants fed their mother’s milk or donor human milk, as there is insufficient evidence of benefits. This recommendation is based on low-quality evidence. 8. VLBW infants should be given 10 ml/kg per day of enteral feeds, preferably expressed breast milk, starting from the first day of life. The remaining fluid requirements should be met with intravenous fluids. This is a weak recommendation relevant to resource-limited settings where total parenteral nutrition is not feasible, supported by low to very low-quality evidence. 9. LBW infants should be exclusively breastfed until six months of age. This is a strong recommendation, although based on very low-quality evidence. 10. LBW infants requiring alternative oral feeding methods should be fed using a cup (or palladai, a cup with a beak) or a spoon. This is a strong situational recommendation relevant to resource-limited settings, supported by moderate-quality evidence. 11. In VLBW infants requiring intragastric tube feeding, the tube may be placed either orally or nasally, depending on the healthcare provider’s preference. This is a weak recommendation based on very low-quality evidence. 12. LBW infants who are predominantly fed using alternative oral feeding methods should be fed based on hunger cues, except when the infant remains asleep for more than three hours since the last feed. This is a weak situational recommendation relevant to settings with adequate healthcare providers, supported by moderate-quality evidence. 13. In VLBW infants requiring alternative oral feeding methods or intragastric tube feeds, feed volumes can be increased by up to 30 ml/kg per day with careful monitoring for feed intolerance. This is a weak recommendation supported by high-quality evidence. 14. For HIV-exposed infants, adding nucleic acid testing (NAT) at birth to existing early infant diagnosis (EID) testing approaches can be considered to identify HIV infection. This is a conditional recommendation based on low-quality evidence. 15. NAT technologies validated for use at or near the point of care can be used for early infant HIV testing. This is a conditional recommendation supported by low-quality evidence. 16. Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) for HIV serology can be used to assess HIV exposure in infants less than four months of age. For infants aged 4–18 months, HIV exposure status should be determined by serological testing in the mother. These are conditional recommendations based on low-quality evidence. 17. RDTs for HIV serology can be used at nine months to rule out HIV infection in asymptomatic HIV-exposed infants. This is a conditional recommendation supported by low-quality evidence. 18. RDTs for HIV serology can be used to diagnose HIV infection in children older than 18 months, following national testing strategies. This is a strong recommendation supported by moderate-quality evidence. 19. Infants born to mothers with HIV who are at high risk of acquiring HIV should receive dual prophylaxis with AZT (twice daily) and NVP (once daily) for the first six weeks of life, regardless of feeding method. This is a strong recommendation supported by moderate-quality evidence. 20. Breastfed infants at high risk of acquiring HIV, including those identified as exposed during the postpartum period, should continue infant prophylaxis for an additional six weeks (total of 12 weeks) using either AZT and NVP or NVP alone. This is a conditional recommendation based on low-quality evidence. 21. Mothers living with HIV should breastfeed for at least 12 months and may continue breastfeeding for up to 24 months or longer while being fully supported for ART adherence. This is a strong recommendation, with low-quality evidence for 12 months and very low-quality evidence for 24 months. 22. Mothers known to be HIV-infected should exclusively breastfeed their HIV-uninfected infants or infants of unknown HIV status for the first six months of life. This is a strong recommendation supported by high-quality evidence. 23. Clinically apparent neonatal seizures lasting more than three minutes or occurring as brief serial seizures should be treated. This is a strong recommendation, although the quality of evidence is not graded. 24. In specialized care facilities with EEG availability, all electrical seizures, even without clinical manifestations, should be treated. This is a strong context-specific recommendation, with the quality of evidence not graded. 25. In neonates with seizures, hypoglycemia should be ruled out and treated before considering antiepileptic drug treatment. This is a strong recommendation, with the quality of evidence not graded. 26. If glucose measurement facilities are unavailable, empirical treatment with glucose should be considered. This is a weak context-specific recommendation, with the quality of evidence not graded. 27. If clinical signs suggest sepsis or meningitis, central nervous system infection should be ruled out with a lumbar puncture and treated with appropriate antibiotics if present. This is a strong recommendation, with the quality of evidence not graded. 28. If lumbar puncture facilities are unavailable, empirical antibiotic treatment should be considered for neonates with clinical signs of sepsis or meningitis. This is a weak context-specific recommendation, with the quality of evidence not graded. 29. Serum calcium should be measured in neonates with seizures (if facilities are available) and treated if hypocalcemia is present. This is a strong context-specific recommendation, with the quality of evidence not graded. 30. In the absence of hypoglycemia, meningitis, hypocalcemia, or other obvious underlying causes, pyridoxine treatment may be considered before antiepileptic drug treatment in specialized centers where this treatment is available. This is a weak context-specific recommendation, with the quality of evidence not graded. 31. Phenobarbital should be used as the first-line agent for treating neonatal seizures and should be readily available in all settings. This is a strong recommendation supported by very low-quality evidence. 32. In neonates with persistent seizures despite maximal tolerated doses of phenobarbital, either midazolam or lidocaine may be used as second-line agents, with lidocaine requiring cardiac monitoring facilities. This is a weak recommendation supported by very low-quality evidence. 33. In neonates with normal neurological examination and/or normal EEG, antiepileptic drugs should be stopped if the neonate has been seizure-free for more than 72 hours. The drugs should be reinstated if seizures recur. This is a weak recommendation supported by very low-quality evidence. 34. In neonates whose seizures are controlled with a single antiepileptic drug, the drug can be discontinued abruptly without tapering the doses. This is a weak recommendation, with the quality of evidence not graded. 35. In neonates requiring more than one antiepileptic drug for seizure control, the drugs may be stopped one by one, with phenobarbital being the last drug to be withdrawn. This is a weak recommendation, with the quality of evidence not graded. 36. In the absence of clinical seizures, neonates with hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy do not require prophylactic treatment with phenobarbital. This is a strong recommendation supported by moderate-quality evidence. 37. Where available, all clinical seizures in the neonatal period should be confirmed by EEG. This is a strong context-specific recommendation, with the quality of evidence not graded. 38. EEG should not be performed solely to determine the etiology in neonates with clinical seizures. This is a strong recommendation, with the quality of evidence not graded. 39. Radiological investigations (ultrasound, CT, MRI) of the cranium/head should not be performed to determine the presence or absence of clinical seizures or to evaluate the efficacy of antiepileptic drug treatment in neonates. This is a strong recommendation, with the quality of evidence not graded. 40. Radiological investigations may be performed as part of a comprehensive evaluation of the etiology of neonatal seizures or to determine prognosis in neonates with seizures. This is a weak context-specific recommendation, with the quality of evidence not graded. 41. Clinicians should ensure that all newborns are routinely monitored for the development of jaundice. Serum bilirubin should be measured in at-risk babies, including those with jaundice on day 1, preterm babies (<35 weeks) with jaundice on day 2, and all babies with yellow palms and soles at any age. This is a strong recommendation supported by very low-quality evidence. 42. Phototherapy should be stopped once serum bilirubin levels are 50 mmol/L (3 mg/dL) or below the phototherapy threshold. This is a weak recommendation, with the quality of evidence not graded. 43. Young neonates with suspected necrotizing enterocolitis should be treated with intravenous or intramuscular ampicillin (or penicillin) and gentamicin as first-line antibiotic treatment for 10 days. This is a strong recommendation supported by low-quality evidence. 44. Infants with confirmed congenital syphilis or those whose mothers had untreated, inadequately treated, or recently treated syphilis should be treated with aqueous benzyl penicillin or procaine penicillin. Dosages include aqueous benzyl penicillin (100,000–150,000 U/kg/day IV for 10–15 days) or procaine penicillin (50,000 U/kg/day IM for 10–15 days). This is a conditional recommendation supported by very low-quality evidence. 45. Clinically normal infants whose mothers had adequately treated syphilis with no signs of reinfection should be closely monitored. If treatment is provided, benzathine penicillin G (50,000 U/kg/day IM as a single dose) is an option. This is a conditional recommendation supported by very low-quality evidence. 46. Neonates with gonococcal conjunctivitis should be treated with one of the following options: ceftriaxone (50 mg/kg IM as a single dose, maximum 150 mg), kanamycin (25 mg/kg IM as a single dose, maximum 75 mg), or spectinomycin.
